idiom_name: ZIO Schedule: Schedule.recurs(n) composed with Schedule.exponential(base).jittered
implementation_notes: In effect-system Scala the backoff schedule is a value rather than a loop: the ZIO reference expresses exactly this pattern as Schedule.recurs(5) combined with Schedule.exponential(100.millis).jittered, consumed by ZIO#retry, where Schedule is a time-aware state machine whose delays are decided by the runtime (and can be tested by simulating time). Composition with && and || lets the same mechanism express 'exponential but at most five times', 'exponential or every 10 seconds' and other combinations without new code. Plain Scala without an effect system falls back to a tail-recursive loop with Thread.sleep and scala.util.Random; the classic loop is still justified in code that must not take a ZIO or cats-effect dependency.
code_sketch:
import zio._

val policy: Schedule[Any, Any, Long] =
  Schedule.recurs(5) <* Schedule.exponential(100.millis).jittered

val result: ZIO[Any, Throwable, String] =
  callDependency.retry(policy)
pitfalls: Schedule.exponential alone never gives up; combine it with a limiting schedule such as recurs, or the retry is unbounded.
Schedule.recurs counts repetitions, so recurs(5) allows five retries in addition to the initial call.
ZIO#retry covers the typed error channel only: defects (thrown exceptions) are not retried unless they are converted into typed errors first.
